en: Regarding the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-artha-ṭīkā*:
"The inexhaustible light of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the infinite wisdom" clarifies that the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is inexhaustible.
"All phenomena are eternally abiding" refers to the qualities such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). The mind...
Regarding the four kinds of bodies free from faults and evils:
this explains why one is able to always maintain a mind free from all afflictions and a body free from birth, old age, sickness, and death.
It means knowing all *īryāpathas* (modes of conduct).
In the language of Han,
"boundary" (jingjie) refers to that which encompasses and sustains all dharmas;
this is the myriad virtues.
Regarding "removing all faults and evils":
it means to thoroughly understand the Dharma and to be fully equipped with all wholesome dharmas.
Because these three meanings are possessed, one attains permanence.
I have long established you in a single verse;
this was spoken by the Buddha.
By doing so, I have performed a meritorious deed.
Furthermore, this is Śrīmālā’s prior request for protection of her person;
this protection of the Dharma is precisely what constitutes the bestowal of a prophecy (vyākaraṇa).
Since it possesses the merit of reverence and praise, [it should be upheld].
Furthermore, he paid his respects and made a request,
seeking that the Tathāgata might cause him to practice the ten thousand virtues; thus,
the Sovereign King was granted a prediction.
This records his supreme fruit within the causal stage:
that he constantly acted as a sovereign king of the gods (Indra).
As for "immeasurable asaṃkhyeya buddhas": [this refers to the number of buddhas he served].
The prediction [of future attainment] depends upon the practice of cultivation.
As for the name "Universal Radiance" (Puguang),
it is a prediction of one's name.
"Tathāgata, Samyaksaṃbuddha" is a designation of his virtuous name.
"There are no evil destinies" means:
This is a record of the land and its disciples.
It briefly records five matters.
Regarding those who received the ten great precepts:
This is the title of the second sutra.
The former [part] refers to the person who receives, and the latter refers to the Dharma that is received.
There is a person capable of receiving it.
Because the Dharma has that which can be received,
"receiving" (shou) constitutes its name.
Because these ten names encompass the myriad phenomena, they are called "great" (da).
Regarding the ten thousand, it is concise;
regarding the one, it is extensive.
There are two types of the "Great Dispersion of the Ten Receptions."
The first is self-practice and the second is transforming others.
The first five precepts and the tenth precept constitute self-practice;
the four intermediate precepts constitute transforming others.
Furthermore, there are two meanings:
the specific and the general;
that is, the ninth is the specific and the tenth is the general.
One who is free from a mind of attachment does not abandon the distant to pursue the intimate;
one who is free from a mind of insatiability delights in constantly preaching the Dharma.
One with an unimpeded mind speaks whenever requested;
"in various places" refers to those respective locations.
In every instance,
those who should be subdued are restrained by means of majestic power.
Those who should be gathered in should be transformed through gentle speech,
so that the Dharma may endure for a long time.
These two dharmas discipline sentient beings;
the Buddhadharma remains long in the world, gods and humans abound,
and those in the fortunate realms increase.
For the sake of these two benefits, they do not abandon them but transform others through them.
As for those who have forgotten the Dharma,
they have forgotten the human qualities of the Mahāyāna.
In total, there are five meanings:
first, the desire for the true Dharma;
second, the upholding of the true Dharma.
The third is called "Desiring to Practice the Mahāyāna";
the fourth is called "Pāramitās";
and the fifth is called "The Beginning of Cultivating Goodness in the Mahāyāna."

One must necessarily possess the mind that seeks excellent desires; once the mind of desire exists, one then takes [the Dharma] up for oneself. Having taken it up for oneself, one desires to uphold and practice the Mahāyāna.
Having practiced the Mahāyāna, one knows that one can reach the fruit, and one knows that there is the capacity to transport [others].
Śrīmālā herself clearly demonstrated that she was certainly able to practice and accomplish these five meanings;
therefore, she stated that she would never forget them.
This was intended to clarify how a practitioner might lose their wholesome qualities.
Therefore, one loses the end by following the beginning,
and loses the beginning by following the end;
the sequence of the intermediate stages clarifies the meaning of this loss.
Regarding "forgetting the Dharma," this clarifies that those who forget the Mahāyāna lose both the beginning and the end.
This is why the term "desire" is not mentioned.
Because the term "appropriation" (parigraha) occurs among the ten types of feeling,
it is mentioned once they have been clarified.
One who is not certain about the Mahāyāna cannot obtain the desire for appropriation.
This clarifies that one loses the end while forgetting the beginning;
thus, the middle is entirely lost.
This is the fifth meaning of the gradual loss of the wholesome.
One will then lose the supreme fruits of the world-transcending noble ones;
following birth into death, one will remain forever an ordinary person.
This is a most grievous matter to avoid.
If one is thus [in this regard],
because one excels in this true principle, it is called the "True Dharma" (saddharma).
Because it can be taken up as the essential within oneself, it is called "appropriation" (parigraha).
Regarding "entering according to what is desired":
being unable to reverse the flow of existence and instead accepting the bodies of the three realms of existence is called "desire.
Regarding "transcending the stage of ordinary beings": [it refers to transcending those who are attached to such desire].
Having turned one's back on the Sage and accepted rebirth,
how could one transcend the stage of an ordinary person?
As for the immeasurable great transgressions:
One loses the victory of the Sage and attains the lowliness of an ordinary person; therefore, it is called a "great transgression.
Regarding "immeasurable benefit and merit":
The various virtues are the fruits of the noble ones.
By practicing the ten perceptions, one then attains them.
As for the ten perceptions:
Thus, because it enters into the state of ordinary beings, both are clarified.
As for "manifesting as my witness," although there are ten names, they collectively encompass all myriad virtues.
Women are weak and inferior, and thus it is said they cannot practice [the path].
Although the Tathāgata knows that others harbor doubts,
he cannot speak of them unless he has personally realized them through direct manifestation.
That which is not beneficial to the meaning is an evil retribution.
As for the raining down of various celestial flowers and the issuing of wondrous sounds:
The two auspicious omens of the flower and the sound signify that whoever takes up these flowers will surely practice the ten [precepts], and whoever hears this sound will surely attain Bodhi.
Those who act accordingly share in this same result.
"Severing Doubt and Seeing Benefits: A Vow to Practice Together with Śrīmālā in the Ten Receptions" is the title of the third sutra.
"The Proclamation of the Three Great Vows" is the name of the third scripture.
Initially, ten names were used to encompass the myriad virtues;
now, with these three names, all are fully subsumed.
This is intended to lead back to the One.
Therefore, by diminishing [self-attachment], one seeks to bring goodness under one's own control.
At the outset, one should speak of receiving [the precepts] with the aim of reaching through eternal kalpas; thus it is called a "vow" (praṇidhāna).
This initial stage constitutes self-cultivation.
Second is outward transformation;
third is the protection of the Dharma.
By means of these roots of goodness...
These are the ten wholesome retributions.
One who attains knowledge of the True Dharma is a wise person;
such a wise person knows that the myriad virtues are worthy of veneration.
Just as all forms are entirely contained within the realm of space— where blue,
yellow, crimson, and purple are subsumed by the realm of space—
so too are the five precepts and all virtues contained within the three vows.
"The three vows are like space, and all virtues are like form.
"Receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he speaks of the Great Vow of Subduing" is the title of the fourth sutra.
One name encompasses ten thousand;
one must receive the essential intent before understanding it.
Although names are not two, they still do not immediately coincide with reality.
To clarify the Way of the One Vehicle is not something that can be easily proclaimed;
it is as "Good" (Śubha) said regarding the constant non-disparagement of others.
To not give rise to any evils is called "subduing.
To gather all beings into one is called "great.
To never abandon them throughout eternal kalpas is called a "vow."
That which is true and without deviation is speech that accords with reason and can certainly be put into practice.
What is called "upholding the true Dharma" is a designation for the sūtras;
there is no separate dharma other than this.
It is said that because there is a beginning and an end, there are two names: "appropriation" and "vow.
Only those who have long planted roots of goodness are able to understand what you have said.
To know all virtues through a single name is not something that can be realized without long-term cultivation.
Now, I shall explain what ought to be explained.
The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time all speak of the myriad virtues.
This clarifies that Śrīmālā’s teaching is the same as that of all Buddhas;
because they desire to cause people to have faith, they accumulate these merits.
"Regarding 'not reaching a limit':
since the skillful exposition of the Dharma is infinite, how could it ever be exhausted?
Wisdom and eloquence are likewise without limit."
This clarifies that the Tathāgata’s wisdom is capable of universal knowledge and discernment, which is inexhaustible;
it is not a matter of the limits of intellectual understanding.
It possesses great merit and great benefit.
"Goodness" refers to merit; "person" refers to benefit.
Herein is revealed the meaning that the bonds of goodness, as numerous as the atoms of the path attained, blaze forth boundlessly.
To further elaborate upon this:
The preceding section has clarified the essence;
now, I wish to provide an elegant illustration of this fruit,
which constitutes its second meaning.
"Attaining all Buddha-dharmas" refers to the dharmas of fruition.
"The eighty-four thousand dharma-gates" refers to...
This is the dharma of causes.
As for "raining down a rain of manifold colors," this is a metaphor for the True Dharma.
It can produce all manner of goodness, raining down colors such as blue and yellow;
goodness has ten thousand varieties of difference,
and this supreme rain is the Dharma.
Being protected from the rain by others and possessing various kinds of jewels are the fruits.
"Raining down immeasurable rewards of merit" refers to the convergence of the fruits [of practice].
"And immeasurable roots of goodness" refers to the same.
This refers to the convergence of causes.
"There is a great accumulation of water" clarifies that the True Dharma is capable of bringing about accomplishment and benefit.
The "Treasury of the Trichiliocosm" is a metaphor for the Mahāyāna.
As for the "four hundred billion," it refers to...
This is a metaphor for the two causes and two fruits.
"The great treasury of realms" refers to the convergence of the great trichiliocosm.
Supernormal powers (abhijñā) are the cause of the untainted (anāsrava).
As for mastery over the mind as one wishes (yatheṣṭavaśitā):
This is a cause of tainted virtue (*sāsrava-kuśala*).
Or rather, the capacity of its fruit cannot be lost.
As for "peaceful security and happiness":
These are the fruits of outflows (*sāsrava*).
Worldly supramundane bliss is the fruit without outflows (*anāsrava*).
This comprises four hundred *koṭis* of explanations.
Regarding the phrase "all that occurs within when the kalpa is completed":
it refers to the initial foundation of goodness.
All that emerges from the True Dharma consists specifically of the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions;
"embracing the True Dharma" is the general designation for these.
Therefore, one is able to give rise to vows.
Furthermore, "like the great earth" is a metaphor for a person;
it refers to one who upholds the Dharma.
Because they are able to carry and support sentient beings, they are like the earth.
They bring the roots of goodness of humans and devas to their ultimate fulfillment by bestowing them upon the Mahāyāna;
this clarifies the person who upholds the Dharma.
It is able to [serve as] the cause and effect of the tainted and untainted wholesome dharmas of sentient beings.
As the mother of worldly dharmas,
it is able to give birth to the fruits of humans, devas, and sages through all manner of wholesome deeds.
This concludes the explanation of the teacher’s capability.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the great earth possesses four treasure-troves," this metaphor clarifies those who receive and uphold the Dharma.
All sentient beings are like the great earth;
the four types of persons are like the four treasuries.
The preceding analogy clarifies that humans possess the capacity for transformative power.
This analogy clarifies the meaning of a person’s capacity to receive.
Having thus explained the correct reception of the True Dharma, [the text] now refers back to the aforementioned person capable of transforming others— the son or daughter of good family.
One who establishes the great earth is one who can lift up those previously burdened and obtain the four kinds of great treasures.
"Upholding the aforementioned True Dharma" means bestowing and granting it; that is,
conferring the Three Refuges and Five Precepts, up to and including the Bodhisattva Precepts.
It also explains the causes and effects of all virtues,
like one who bestows the seven treasures within a treasury.
Such are the sentient beings who obtain the great treasure.
This refers to those who receive the Dharma;
it includes all men and women who have embraced the True Dharma.
This refers to those capable of transforming others.
One who attains these rare and marvelous merits is one who has formed a karmic bond with a Dharma-transmitting teacher.
This clarifies that the Dharma is the meaning of "jewel."
The "great treasure store" refers to one who upholds the true Dharma;
this clarifies that the person is the meaning of the "store.
The word for "person" (*pudgala*) should have been mentioned, but it is omitted here.
The explanation of the meaning of the disciples who receive the Dharma is hereby concluded.
Regarding "upholding the true Dharma"— one who upholds the true Dharma—
this is the third clarification of the identity between the Dharma and its characteristics.
The first phrase refers to the mind that is capable of embracing;
the second phrase reiterates this.
"The True Dharma is no different" means:
This clarifies that the mind is not different from phenomena;
there is no one who upholds the true Dharma who is distinct [from it].
This clarifies that phenomena are not different from the mind.
The True Dharma is itself that which upholds the True Dharma.
This clarifies that the True Dharma is none other than the mind;
because they are known to be non-different, it can be authenticated.
Furthermore, one should understand that the mind can likewise seal the Dharma; since they are not different, it is possible to know this through sealing.
That which is the non-different *pāramitā* is the emergence of the True Dharma.
Although the preceding section provided an esoteric explanation, its substance has not yet been fully understood.
Therefore, I shall clarify it further by means of concrete phenomena;
the phrasing will not differ, and the meaning will not differ from what was stated above.
Therefore, regarding the elucidation of its meaning in six aspects:
the general purport of this sutra clarifies that the practice of the six pāramitās is what the bodhisattva undertakes.
Regarding "men and women who embrace the true Dharma," this clarifies the teacher.
Those who should be matured through giving [are as follows].
Seeing sentient beings who can be taught to practice giving,
those who are matured through giving are the former individuals who receive and practice the Dharma.
This is the Dharma of giving.
It extends even to the relinquishing of the limbs and joints of the body,
as well as the head, eyes, marrow, and brain.
For those who first embark on the path, they proceed from the easy to the difficult;
at first they renounce a single thread or a single strand of silk,
and in the middle stage they renounce clothing, food, kingdoms, and cities.
Later, he renounced his wife, children, body, and life;
because he transcended the initial and intermediate stages, it is said "up to and including" (*yāvat*).
From this point downward, all five perfections (*pāramitā*) are of this same nature.
To protect another's intention means that if one is able to relinquish a thread, one teaches them to relinquish the thread;
even if it comes to one's own body and life, one teaches them to relinquish them.
If one is unable to relinquish the body,
yet instructs another to do so by means of their own life,
they will certainly be unable to practice it; this does not constitute "fulfilling the excellence of others" and is not called "protective guardianship."
Those beings whom he has brought to maturity and who establish the True Dharma practice the dharma of relinquishment;
this is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
"Clarity" is precisely "meaning.
The mind that is able to receive [the teaching] and the dharma that is relinquished—though these two meanings differ, their substance is not distinct.
Thus, the meaning of their oneness is clear.
It should be known that all treatises generally comprise five types of discourse:
first, the inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*),
which consists of those who skillfully understand the sūtras and śāstras of the Buddha-dharma.
Second, the treatises on external luminosity (*bāhyavidyā*),
which consist of a thorough understanding of the scriptures, prophecies, and treatises of non-Buddhist schools.
Third, the treatises on logic (*hetuvidyā*).
He was well-versed in how all phenomena arise through causal conditions.
He was also proficient in the four treatises on grammar and phonology,
being skilled in understanding the various differences among regional dialects and sounds.
The fifth is the treatise on arts and crafts (*śilpa-vidyā*).
It refers to being well-versed in mechanical devices, wooden automata, illusions, transformations, and incantations.
This includes all forms of craftsmanship.
He knows that all things are like mechanical contrivances and magical illusions.
Furthermore, regarding all matters, he skillfully understands the reasons for the good and evil of the actions performed.
By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he further expounds upon the great meaning.
The fourth clarifies the identity of the person and the dharma.
The person and the dharma ought to be different in essence;
now, we clarify their identity, which must necessarily be established by refuting [the opposing view].
"Upholding the True Dharma.
This single phrase clarifies the Dharma.
Regarding "upholding the True Dharma":
This single phrase clarifies the person.
"There is no difference in the upholding of the true Dharma" clarifies that the person is not different from the Dharma.
"There is no one who upholds the true Dharma who is distinct [from it].
This clarifies that the Dharma is not separate from the person;
the son or daughter of good family who upholds the true Dharma is themselves the upholding of the true Dharma.
The first phrase refers to the person;
the second phrase refers to the Dharma.
This is because the person is itself the Dharma.
Furthermore, the principle that the Dharma is identical to the person should be understood as being the same as in the preceding chapter.
As for why the person and the Dharma can be mutually identical:
although the five aggregates, the various bases, and even up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñā) are each distinct in their individual essence.
This is what constitutes the Dharma.
The five aggregates (skandhas) and the various sense bases (āyatanas) together constitute the person.
Because of the distinction between the collective and the individual, there is the differentiation between the person and the Dharma.
Because the particular is treated as the universal, they are identical as one.
Regarding the phrase "the son of good family who abandons the three parts":
this clarifies that a person who practices goodness is, in essence, the Dharma itself.
Thus, one knows that the True Dharma is neither evil nor indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding the phrase "the future limit of birth and death" (*saṃsāra-paścimānta*):
in the future world, birth and death are inexhaustible.
I vow to attain the fruit of sagehood so that my capacity may equal theirs.
Although old age, sickness, and death are recorded as characteristics of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body,
when speaking from the perspective of the ultimate state, the Buddha possesses the designation of "sage" (śramaṇa), and thus the sense of "person" (pudgala) applies.
Because its essence is the principle of goodness, it possesses the meaning of "Dharma" (dharma).
Furthermore, according to another interpretation, that which aspires upward to seek the fruit of Buddhahood and is able to relinquish the three parts is "Dharma."
The other two categories are likewise.
Thus, when it says "a son of good family who abandons these three," it refers to a superior person.
One who upholds the true Dharma is the Dharma itself;
one who binds others is the Dharma itself.
Furthermore, O World-Honored One, regarding good sons and daughters,
the fifth point clarifies their protection of the Dharma:
those who engage in factionalism and contentious litigation.
The fourfold assembly,
each following their own kin and old acquaintances, collectively engaged in both right and wrong, committing various evils;
they caused destruction and brought about dissension.
They do not allow for disputes;
they transform others either through wholesome means or through the power of their majesty.
As for "being without guile," since one employs correctness with straightforwardness, how could there be any crookedness?
As for "being without deception," [it means that one does not mislead others].
If it is evil, one speaks of it as evil;
if it is good, one speaks of it as good—what falsehood is there in this? It is not deceptive.
This is an illustration by means of a simile;
it is not like a phantom or something feigned that lacks reality.
One who loves and delights in the True Dharma.
To cause the True Dharma to abide long in the world,
one who upholds the True Dharma is able to maintain it.
Those who enter the circle of the Dharma friends are those who transform those involved in disputes and litigation,
and those who practice together in goodness.
Those who have been granted predictions [of enlightenment] are said to be people who practice goodness;
they are predicted by the Buddha. How can one not abandon the evils of contention and strife?
"Furthermore, he fully knows and sees.
This briefly clarifies that the Tathāgata possesses these five virtues;
it should be understood that his disciples will certainly be able to protect the Dharma.
It is because they have not yet reached fulfillment that they seek realization.
Those who give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy through the power of great diligence—
this is the sixth Tathāgata fulfilling what was spoken.

it begins with what has long been victorious;
