However, one who is able to relinquish these three is superior to one who does not.
That one should embrace the Three Right Dharmas and reveal them to sentient beings—
this is the exhortation of the Tathāgata.
From now until the Buddha preaches the Dharma to teach and transform others, leading them to cultivate goodness,
one should employ the True Dharma.
Such is this great benefit.
This explains the meaning of benefiting others:
that all sentient beings shall be free from all evils.
Such is one of great merit.
It is the fulfillment of the ten thousand virtues.
Such a great fruit is that which can bring about the fruit of Buddhahood.
Regarding the benefits attained that cannot reach an ultimate limit,
it is said that both bondage and conditioned formations are inexhaustible.
As for what you have now further stated:
This is the title of the fifth sutra.
It is called "The True Principle," which is not within the reach of those on the stage of training;
it must be by the Buddha’s command that one dares to speak of it. One maintains the essence while altering the name, receiving and expounding upon it.
As one who upholds the True Dharma and adheres to the Mahāyāna,
having received this command,
how could I fail to speak?
May that which is spoken necessarily accord with principle;
may its principles be vast and its words great, encompassing all without exception— the meaning of the One Vehicle.
It is now clearly revealed.

Regarding the statement that "the Mahāyāna gives birth to all supramundane wholesome dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas," this extends from here until the point of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).
To clarify the entry into causes,
and about to clarify the entry itself,
one first speaks of the wholesome exit.
If one emerges from this and returns to enter it, that is "is-ness" (tathatā).
Reaching the pond is like the Mahāyāna;
the eight rivers are like the four causes and four fruits.
The four types of people, by virtue of their roots of goodness, all enter the Mahāyāna.
"The duration of the True Dharma" refers to the number of kalpas for which the Buddha-dharma remains in the world.
When the True Dharma perishes,
it passes into the Semblance Dharma;
when the Semblance Dharma perishes, the Buddha-dharma is extinguished altogether.
Regarding the statement "spoken for the sake of the Mahāyāna":
the persistence of the Dharma and the extinction of the Dharma are themselves the Mahāyāna; this is intended to cause those of the two vehicles to understand that these are not different from it.
This refers to the three dharmas of the Prātimokṣa.
The four dharmas of a bhikṣu have the same meaning though different names;
they share the single meaning of being able to obstruct evil.
*Vinaya* and *Prātimokṣa* are their alternative names.
Furthermore, another new interpretation holds that both are Mahāyāna and thus identical in meaning (*artha-eka*).
*Vinaya* and *mokṣa* are different names for the practices of the two vehicles;
this is precisely what the Mahāyāna scholars clarify as being identical in meaning.
The correct principle is that all paths lead to the same destination; there is no distinction between great and small dharmas.
To leave the household life according to the Buddha constitutes the five dharmas, and to receive full ordination likewise constitutes a dharma.
As for the question "Why is this so?":
Why is it that the *mokṣa-vinaya* (liberation-discipline) of the two vehicles is itself the Mahāyāna?
The following explanation clarifies that because the Buddha attained the state of renunciation (*pravrajyā*), one knows that *mokṣa* is indeed the Mahāyāna.
Next, as for the question "Why is this so?":
Why is it that the two vehicles have no distinct dharma upon which they can rely for renunciation?
The intent of the explanation is that, by relying on the Buddha-dharma, one knows there is no distinct dharma [apart from it].
If the followers of the Two Vehicles possessed their own distinct dharmas,
how could they rely upon the Mahāyāna Buddha-dharma?
That an Arhat takes refuge in the Buddha and Dharma indicates that he has departed from the realm of nirvāṇa and clearly enters the stage of fruition.

It was previously stated that the two vehicles possess a final dharma; however, upon examining the reality of this matter, one must look upward toward the vast path of cultivation to seek the ultimate realization of the Buddha.
Therefore, those of the two fruits enter into the One Vehicle.
Regarding those who possess fear:
although it was previously said that by eliminating all evils one is without [fear], if there is still fear, it is known that evil has not yet been exhausted. Why is this so?
"Why is there fear?
This explains the meaning of "fear" with respect to one who practices nothing at all.
Although there is no longer birth-and-death in discrete segments (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*), one still dwells on the ground of fear because one knows that [afflictions] are not yet exhausted.
This is illustrated by the example of a person grasping a sword.
This is cited as an analogy.
The celestial Māras are like people; birth and death are like swords; and the two vehicles are like those who have already [been wounded].
Regarding the absence of ultimate bliss:
even the two vehicles still harbor the suffering of fear, and the bliss they attain is but a small portion, insufficient for fulfillment.
Why is this? Why is it not ultimate bliss? Because the Blessed One relies on that which is not sought as a refuge.
This explains the meaning of why [the former] is not ultimate.
The World-Honored One is fearless because he does not rely on external things;
he seeks no refuge for himself other than the Two Vehicles. Those who possess fear seek refuge in the Tathāgata, yet they cannot take external things as their place of refuge.
This is an analogy used to illustrate how sentient beings who lack a refuge experience various forms of fear;
it is like a person who does not rely upon a king.
A son does not rely upon his father;
likewise, the five realms of existence—including humans and devas—do not rely upon the Buddha.
In the end, there is fear everywhere and no joy at all.
Because there are remaining dharmas of birth that have not been exhausted, there are those who still undergo birth;
this clarifies that the four wisdoms of the two vehicles are not yet ultimate.
Because they are not ultimate, one enters the One Vehicle.
Since the transformation [of existence] still persists,
how can it be called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)?
Because there remains further holy life (*brahmacarya*) to be accomplished, it is not yet pure.
That which has not yet attained the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is called the "remaining brahmacarya.
Because the evil of the two vehicles' nirvāṇa is not yet exhausted, it cannot be called the purely pure dharma.
This explains that it is not the ultimate, exhaustive knowledge (*anupadhiśeṣa-jñāna*).
That is to say, as long as one has not reached the ultimate and there remains something yet to be accomplished, one must still engage in practice;
it cannot be called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
Regarding the statement that "because one has not yet crossed over to the other shore, there must be something to be severed":
this refers to the ground of abiding in ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*); this fetter must be eliminated and cannot be termed "unconditioned wisdom" (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*).
The Abhidharmikas briefly explain two kinds of wisdom.
These are the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). In this sutra, these four knowledges are not different;
they are presented as two by combining cause and effect.
These are established as four because cause and effect are distinct.
"Not accomplishing all merits" explains the phrase "having birth."
"Measurable qualities" explains the phrase "not being exclusive," while "inconceivable qualities" explains the phrase "having something to be accomplished."
Regarding the phrase "there are further faults," the commentary explains that there is something yet to be severed.

From the mention of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas up to the explanation of the Ultimate Vehicle (Paramārthayāna), the textual analysis concerning the purpose for entering the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna) comprises eight distinct categories.
First, it clarifies that birth and death have not yet been eliminated;
second, it clarifies that afflictions are not yet exhausted;
third, it clarifies the distinct nature of the process of taking birth.
Fourth, what they know is not comprehensive;
fifth, what they have attained is not sufficient;
sixth, what they have severed is not the same.
7. It clarifies the profound distinction between the two types of knowledge.
8. It clarifies the distinctiveness of the Three Jewels.

Since it concludes with the mention of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, it states that they do not undergo further existence, thereby clarifying that their cycle of birth and death has not yet been eliminated.
Although those of the Two Vehicles are free from the death and rebirth of the segmented realm (*paricchinna-bhava*),
they still possess the cessation of the death and rebirth of the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).
This transformation cannot be extinguished except by the One Vehicle.
Therefore, one should enter into the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
From the point that all afflictions are not yet exhausted up until the teaching on the possession of supreme great power, it is said that the afflictions are not exhausted.
Although those of the Two Vehicles have severed the afflictions of the three realms and the four abodes, [the afflictions are still not fully exhausted].
There still remains the affliction of the ground where ignorance dwells;
if one wishes to sever it,
the merit arises from the One Vehicle, and because it must be eliminated, one knows that [the Bodhisattva] has entered it.

Furthermore, as taught by the World-Honored One, the process of taking up birth is explained as being conditioned by the four graspings (*upādāna*), which are themselves rooted in the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*).
Although those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) lack the four graspings,
their tainted wholesome karma (*sāsrava-kuśala-karma*) still has the ground of ignorance as its condition.
Taking uncontaminated wholesome karma as its cause,
it gives rise to the death-and-rebirth of the transformation of dharma-practice;
because of the power of this Single Vehicle (ekayāna), one enters [nirvana] once again after having transcended this death-and-rebirth.

From the World-Honored One, the Arhat, the Pratyekabuddha, and up to the Bodhisattva in their final body, they have practiced the path with remainder and their exposition of what is to be known is incomplete.
Although those of the Two Vehicles know the dharmas of the Three Realms and the Four Noble Truths, [their understanding remains limited].
In general, they have not yet known the Four Noble Truths beyond the triple world.
Because knowing those truths brings one to the ultimate consummation of the One Vehicle, they enter [the path] once again.
This is the One Vehicle.
From this point on, it is called "attaining a small portion of nirvāṇa. The "equal taste" refers to the taste of liberation; what has been attained is not yet sufficient.
For those of the two vehicles, the scriptures state that they attain *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder), which is [merely] what has been attained in reality.
There are those who have attained the remainderless state by only a small portion;
because they practice according to the One Vehicle, it is known that they shall again enter the One Vehicle.
This has been definitively declared by the World-Honored One, from the point of not severing and not perfecting the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*).
This explains the difference in what is abandoned.
Those of the Two Vehicles have already severed the afflictions of the four abodes within the three realms to attain the fruit of Arhatship.
Bodhisattvas, however, sever the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), exhausting it completely and ultimately to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Because those on the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas must ultimately reach the stage of Buddhahood, they enter [the path] again.
From the World-Honored One’s knowledge that there is no further existence, there are two kinds which culminate in the infinite and uninterrupted.
It is said that there is a profound distinction between the two types of wisdom:
the wisdom of the two vehicles knows the exhaustion of death through分段 (fen-duan, *pariccheda*),
while the Tathāgata knows the exhaustion of death through 變易 (bian-yi, *pariṇāmiki*).
The exhaustion of death in its segmented form is not ultimate wisdom;
the exhaustion of all death is called ultimate wisdom.
Because these two types of persons know for themselves that they must cultivate and study the One Vehicle while looking up in aspiration toward Buddha-wisdom, they enter once again.
From the time the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, dwelt in the ultimate truth (paramārtha) without limit or end,
he clarified that the Three Jewels are distinct.
The Three Jewels upon which the two vehicles rely differ in their essential nature.
Furthermore, it is impermanent because it is the single substance of the Three Jewels upon which Bodhisattvas rely;
yet it is also permanent.
Because those of the Two Vehicles must rely on this single, eternally abiding substance to practice the One Vehicle and seek that eternally abiding substance, they enter [this teaching] once again.
Observing liberation,
one personally perceives the diligent departure from the afflictions of the four abodes and the four wisdoms regarding the death and rebirth of the segmented existence.
"Ultimate" refers to these four knowledges: "My births are exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence after this.
These four names are obtained because death by way of limited segments has been ended.
Regarding the "place of rest":
it is called "rest" because there is no death involving the fragmentation of the aggregates.
This is for the sake of those who have not yet understood the definitive meaning.
The former statement that the two vehicles have no further ultimate attainment is an expedient explanation intended to guide sentient beings.
As for those who undergo death through the breaking up of the physical body:
Bound by the fetters of the three realms, they lack freedom;
their lifespans, whether long or short, are identical across the various realms and stages.
As for the inconceivable:
The Dharma-body is unbound and dwells at will, manifesting transformations without fixed direction; those of inferior and ignorant capacity do not perceive this.
As for "vain and false sentient beings," they do not know the Four Noble Truths and lack the true wisdom that is free from outflows.
As for the "mind-made body" (manomaya-kāya),
it is known that its spiritual transformations occur in every thought-moment and are not subject to disbelief.
As for the phrase "because of death by segmentation":
The word "wu" (non-) should be present here.
"My births are exhausted" refers to the attainment of the four knowledges (*jñāna*) upon the cessation of death within the realm of segmented existence (*prādeśika-maraṇa*).
Since the explanation of the meaning is concluded, it is therefore summarized as follows: "There are two kinds of afflictions":
the first is the four abodes, and the second is the affliction of the ground of ignorance-abode (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*).
This refers to the afflictions of the abiding stages (*sthiti-bhūmi*) and the arising afflictions (*utthāna-kleśa*).

From this point downward, the names for the meaning of "affliction" (*kleśa*) consist of five categories: four are named the "abiding stages" (*catvāraḥ sthiti-bhūmayaḥ*), and two are named "arising afflictions."
The third is named *Ganges-sand*;
the fourth is named *Supreme*;
the fifth is named *Ground of Abiding in Ignorance*.
Although there are five names, there are actually two entities.
When the four dwellings have already arisen,
these are called "different names for a single entity."
The ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is the second.
Since the two categories—those exceeding the sands of the Ganges and those that are universal—each have both a general essence and specific distinctions, there are four [types].
They are called "abiding" (*vāsa*) because they remain perpetually undispelled throughout kalpas.
That which can give rise to subsequent thoughts is called the "ground" (bhūmi).
When the mind is currently functioning, it is called "arising.
The essence of all these thoughts is as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
That which is capable of producing all phenomena is called "superior.
Because it does not arise from the mind, it is called "non-associated.
Because it cannot be perceived through investigation, it is called "beginningless."
Not knowing the true principle is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Having existed throughout vast eons, it is designated by the character for "abiding" (*sthiti*);
because it can give rise [to subsequent states] without ceasing, it is named "ground" (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, it is called "as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" because its substance is manifold;
alternatively, it is called "supreme" because it is the source of all dharmas.
As for the "ground of the abiding of ignorance":
This is the habit-energy of afflictions.
The obscuration of darkness from the eighth stage through to the tenth stage is termed ignorance (*avidyā*).
For the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body, merely severing [this ignorance] so that it does not arise is called "non-conjunction" (*apratisaṃyukta*).
The stage following the four *vihāra-bhūmis* is called "abiding" (*sthiti*).
It is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*) because subtle [defilements] still remain and are thus able to give rise to coarse ones.
Furthermore, another interpretation states:
Regarding the fetters of the four abodes within the three realms that belong to the past,
they cannot directly give rise to present activity through the mind.
Furthermore, another interpretation states:
The beginning of sentient beings must involve spiritual deliberation.
Deliberation has degrees of clarity and obscurity;
phenomena have degrees of coarseness and subtlety.
One should thoroughly know all phenomena, both coarse and subtle.
Because the mind is dull, it consequently reaches only the coarse;
yet no coarse phenomenon possesses the nature of being an object of the mind.
This lack of knowledge is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
That which does not engage with mental deliberation is called non-associated (*viprayukta*).
Regarding that which possesses the greatest power, there are two kinds.
First, because it is difficult to sever;
second, because it is that which was originally bestowed [upon them],
intended to cause people to feel weary of it.
These three stages are the stages of the three vehicles.
Those three kinds of mind-made bodies are immeasurable in the future.
That which has already occurred in the past or present is called "this";
that which is yet to be received in the future is called "that.
It is not the case that they are different because [the latter] clarifies what arises prior to receiving [the fruit].
Regarding those [afflictions] to be abandoned in the eighth stage:
the reason they are said to be "abandoned" is to clarify that the Buddha has already abandoned them.
Because the three types of persons who undergo rebirth have not yet eliminated [the afflictions], there is birth and death.
It is only when this is suddenly absent that the stage of Buddhahood (buddhabhūmi) receives its name.
As for "the untainted [outflows] being inexhaustible":
Although these three types of persons are able to eliminate the fetter of "going," because their outflows have not yet been fully exhausted,
they are mentioned in the subsequent passage.
This is precisely the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
Regarding "those various phenomena," these are the boundless noble truths (*ananta-āryasatya*).
It still remains outside the scope;
furthermore, it is not a single [entity].
As for that which ought to be abandoned:
This is the ground where ignorance dwells.
It is called "liberation with remaining defects" because the state attained through the cessation of分段死 (segmented death) has not yet been permanently eliminated.
Regarding those who possess residual purity:
although they have not severed the afflictions of the stage of ignorance (avidyā-āvasthika-kleśa) within the four stages of dwelling,
they have accomplished residual merit.
Although one has attained the ten knowledges and various wholesome merits, one has not yet attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
To understand that there remains further suffering up to the remaining path,
one first clarifies the three matters thus obtained.
Others, in turn, state that their knowledge is incomplete;
these are called those who have attained a limited nirvāṇa.

Because they have eliminated the four abodes and the death-and-rebirth of the segmented realm, they receive the name "nirvāṇa"; yet because the essence [of this state] is not yet fulfilled, it is termed "limited."
To know all suffering refers to the suffering of coarse phenomena;
the same applies to the other three truths.
That by which one clearly knows is this:
that the nirvāṇa attained through the full extent of wisdom is necessarily complete.
As for "impermanence destroying the world":
Birth and death are the fruit of retribution;
impermanence and sickness are the world's causes of birth and death.
"To attain eternal nirvāṇa" means to attain the Buddha’s fulfillment of ultimate nirvāṇa.
"In the world that lacks protection" refers to...
One cannot avoid the four māras.
Regarding those who have no refuge in the world:
the people of saṃsāra are not to be relied upon.
Why is this? Because how could the Tathāgata be able to protect that which is not to be relied upon?
There is no superiority or inferiority among dharmas.
The ten powers and fearlessnesses are alike in being without high or low.
Regarding "wisdom is equal," it means there is no distinction between the knowledge of all modes, the knowledge of non-arising, and spontaneous wisdom.
"Purity" and so forth mean being equally free from afflictions.
"Liberation" and so forth mean being free from birth and death.
Regarding "the samādhi of equal flavor" (*samā-rasa*): it refers to the stage of fulfillment where there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority.
As for "the flavor of liberation," it is called "equal" because there is no burden and all states are uniform.
If the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is neither severed nor fully exhausted,
then before explaining its severance, one must first state its faults.
This refers to "not attaining a single flavor" (*ekarasa*).
One does not obtain the flavor of the Buddha’s liberation;
this is the first fault.
As for that which should be abandoned but is not abandoned:
That the various delusions of ignorance have not yet been extinguished is the second fault.
Regarding that which ought to be attained but is not:
One does not attain the myriad virtues;
this is the third fault.
Regarding that which should be realized but is not realized:
It cannot establish the Buddha’s Dharma-body;
these are the four faults.
Therefore, that which is the accumulation of the ground of the dwelling of ignorance—
It gathers together the many faults of the assembly.
Furthermore, it submerges the substance of ignorance, which is manifold,
and gives rise to all those who practice the path of cultivation.
This refers to the cultivation of all untainted (*anāsrava*) states.
This clarifies the wisdom capable of severing [afflictions].
Regarding "severing the afflictions and the higher afflictions": [it means] severing the afflictions and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
This explains that which is to be abandoned.
As for the aforementioned afflictions,
they either obstruct the divine mind from attaining clarity and purity.
"Śamatha" refers to the wisdom that establishes the objects of śamatha and vipaśyanā based on the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).
"Dhyāna" refers to the various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of the four dhyānas.
"Samāpatti" refers to the four meditative attainments (*catasraḥ samāpattayaḥ*).
Skillful means (upāya) is the wisdom of seeking;
wisdom (jñāna) is ultimate wisdom.
The fruit consists of the three fruits of humans and devas.
Because the fruits of the Path constitute the causes for the three vehicles of humans and devas, and because they possess the power of either cause or fruit, they are called "powers" (*bala*).
These are the ten powers (*daśabala*);
the fearlessnesses are the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*).
"All are established upon the ground of the abiding of ignorance" (avidyā-vāsabhūmi).
This clarifies the cause for the arising of the characteristics of afflictions;
such is the general purport of this sutra.
Because the ground of the abiding of ignorance is the source of all fetters,
the nature of all phenomena that arise is such that they begin subtly and become coarse later;
whereas the path for severing these fetters begins with the coarse and proceeds to the subtle.
By these two meanings, it is known that the ground of the abiding of ignorance gives rise to the four grounds of abiding.
As for the self-arising of the ground of the abiding of ignorance,
it is subtle because it is severed by the diamond-like [samādhi].
Down to the eighth stage, that which is abandoned is considered coarse;
thus, even a single hair’s breadth of existence arises from it.
All arising of higher afflictions is caused by the *avidyāvāsabhūmi* (the ground of the latency of ignorance), taking the *avidyāvāsabhūmi* as its condition.
The higher afflictions pertain generally to the four abodes and the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*).
With respect to the four abodes, they act as conditions because they are remote;
with respect to the ground of ignorance, they act as causes because they are proximate.
Regarding the "stage of beginningless ignorance that is dissociated from the mind," its name is mentioned here because it is intended to clarify its abandonment.
As for "that which is maintained" and "that which is established":
To speak of their faults:
all afflictions, the four abodes, those arising as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and ignorance.
As for the higher afflictions:
Alternatively, if all phenomena are briefly explained as being twofold, then when these two are excluded, all five are extinguished.
One who attains unimpeded penetration regarding all phenomena is one who skillfully understands the principles of all dharmas.
"One who is free from all faults and evils" refers to one who is without afflictions and the cycle of birth and death.
"One who has attained all merits" refers to...
It is the complete perfection of all virtues.
As for the Dharma King and the Lord of Dharma,
once the ground of abiding in ignorance has been severed and extinguished, they are then able to be fully endowed with them.
These are the three meanings.
Once these three meanings are fully possessed,
one attains Buddhahood and governs the Dharma as King.
To have superior things as one's master means to attain mastery;
to be uniquely transcendent and victorious so as not to be subjugated by external things.
"My births have been exhausted; I shall not undergo further existence.
This clarifies that the Tathāgata is fully endowed with four meanings, being without remainder, ultimate, and supremely perfect.
It is not as with the Two Vehicles, which possess both surplus and deficiency;
therefore, the World-Honored One has given a definitive answer.
This concludes the clarification that the Buddha is ultimately complete, whereas the Two Vehicles are not yet sufficient.
Only when one’s discourse is rational, non-deceptive, and firmly established can it truly be called "fearless speech.
Regarding the statement that "the knowledge of not undergoing further existence is of two kinds," this clarifies the two fruits.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise termed "not subject to further existence.
This means that the Tathāgata is the unsurpassed tamer;
hereafter, the lion’s roar is spoken to clarify the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Among the ten titles [of a Buddha], this briefly explains two.
Regarding "subduing the faults of the mind and the four māras":
it means that all evils have been completely eliminated.
"To attain the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata" means that what is attained is complete and fulfilled.
"All *jñeyas*" (objects of knowledge) refers to...
This is the objective sphere.
This clarifies that the causes for all phenomena to be known are complete;
beyond this, there is nothing further to be produced.
In the stage of Buddhahood, one no longer cultivates the myriad virtues.
As for the stage of non-attainment,
it is ultimate fulfillment wherein there is nothing further to be sought.
"Observation with unimpeded wisdom" is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
"Not depending on others" means...
These dharmas are all known to have vanished; what is there to consult?
"Crossing over the fear of birth and death" clarifies that those of the Two Vehicles possess the wisdom of not undergoing further existence.
Because one eliminates birth-and-death in discrete segments, it is called "crossing over.
Because one will not undergo further rebirth,
it is called "not receiving a subsequent existence."
Regarding "attaining the bliss of liberation in succession":
having eliminated [defilements] through the stage of gradual severance, one subsequently attains *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it refers to the sequence whereby the subtle bliss of the two vehicles serves as the preliminary stage for the bliss of the Tathāgata.
"One who has attained the contemplation of not undergoing further existence" is another name for a wise person.
"The foremost one who finds rest."
Only then does one first escape from calamity.
This is the initial stage of death within the realm of segmented existence (*pariccheda-maraṇa*);
it is the first minor happiness, not yet having attained the eternal departure into great bliss.
Furthermore, another interpretation is that the two vehicles consider themselves to possess the foremost and supreme Dharma.
"Abiding in the stage of nirvana" refers to the stage of the place of rest.
Regarding the stage previously attained by them:
when the Tathāgata first taught the Four Noble Truths, those of the Two Vehicles severed the fetters of the four abodes within the three realms;
having exhausted these, they cast off their final bodies and attained nirvana without remainder.
Since of old, one has clarified what is called "true names," and from the ground previously attained up to the stage of clear illumination, there is still moment-to-moment change and transformation;
thus, one spontaneously becomes aware of birth and death.
There is a further stage from which one shall attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
As for the reason why,
Śrīmālā explains the meaning of what should be understood.
Since the Three Vehicles are ultimately one, how could one who has thoroughly investigated their own practice not know this?
That "this is the Buddha Vehicle" clarifies the meaning of attaining Buddhahood through one's own wisdom.
Regarding that which is the realm of nirvāṇa:
the supreme and transcendent path is called bodhi;
the complete elimination of all burdens is called nirvāṇa.
The various names by which it is sought correspond to its manifestations; although the three meanings of the *dharmakāya* differ, their essence is one.
Thus, when one attains the power of the vehicle of the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*, the ultimate One Vehicle brings all activity to rest.
Thus we know that the Two Vehicles have not yet attained the ultimate designation.
"No difference from the Tathāgata, no difference from the Dharmakāya" clarifies that the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is one.
Those who have attained the ultimate Dharmakāya and those who have reached the ultimate One Vehicle—these two phrases are cited to clarify that it is boundless and uninterrupted.
The Buddha-body is eternally abiding and manifests throughout the ten directions; thus it is called "boundless. Because every thought-moment is subject to extinction, it is called "uninterrupted."
That "the Tathāgata abides for no limited duration, abiding equally throughout the future limit" clarifies that the essence of the Dharma is eternal.
That "his great compassion is limitless and his consolation of the world is limitless" [clarifies the same].
These two lines clarify that the transformation [of sentient beings] extends infinitely.
Regarding the phrase "this is called one who speaks well of the Tathāgata":
it is called "well" because one who proclaims that the Tathāgata’s transformation extends infinitely attains the reality of Buddhahood.

If one were to say that the Tathāgata’s transformation is exhausted at the twin trees, one would lose the reality of the Buddha and could not be called virtuous. That which is inexhaustible and eternally abiding is what is designated as the essence of the Tathāgata.
This [teaching of] permanence is truly the Buddha’s reality and is indeed virtuous.
To say that the Tathāgata’s life-span has ended at the twin trees and that his body is only sixteen feet tall is not called virtuous.
That which is the refuge for all the world is the Dharma-body, which is eternal and capable of being truly realized; those who rely upon this are the most truly real.
Since time immemorial, those of the Two Vehicles have taken refuge in the sixteen-foot manifested and transformation Buddha, regarding him as the reality.
Now, the Buddha who preaches the Dharma as the eternally abiding Dharmakāya is the Mahāsattva.
Thus, we know that those of the Two Vehicles have not yet returned to the True Buddha.
For this reason, they have not yet crossed over from the world.
Birth and death have not yet been eliminated.
Those who do not rely on the world do not rely [on it] because their virtue is not yet fulfilled.
"Acting as an inexhaustible refuge equal to the future limit" means that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is coextensive with the end of time,
constantly serving as a refuge for sentient beings.
"The place of eternal refuge, the one who is the eternal refuge" refers to the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One;
he is the Buddha of the Dharma-body.

This concludes the explanation of the Buddha Jewel as the true substratum, which is eternally abiding. "Dharma" refers to the teaching of the One Vehicle path; "Sangha" refers to the assembly of the Three Vehicles.
This clarifies that the Dharma and Sangha taught in the past were not true, for the myriad virtues constitute the Dharma Jewel.
Those of the three vehicles regard this as the Sangha Jewel;
this clarifies that it is the twofold vehicle (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) upon which they have relied since ancient times.
One who has not yet sought refuge in the ultimate sense has not yet requested the eternal, single-essence Dharma and Sangha;
such a person is called "partial."
Although it is said that this impermanence is [the teaching of] a sage and may thus be provisionally relied upon, why is this so?
Because it is only a partial [teaching].
Regarding the statement that one attains the ultimate dharma through the teaching of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) path-dharma:
the "dharma" here refers to a partial aspect of the teaching;
it is known as partial because it serves as a cause for the ultimate.
Above this, there is no further teaching of the Dharma of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) through which one might attain the ultimate state;
on the stage of Buddhahood, there is nothing further to be sought.
As for those of the Three Vehicles (triyāna), they possess fear.
The "partial" (śrāvaka) refers to those who have not yet eliminated birth and death nor exhausted their afflictions;
because they seek liberation from all evils, practice myriad virtues, and advance toward the Unsurpassed Way, they are called "partial."
Therefore, the two bases of objects are limited;
the bases of discerning the Dharma and the Sangha are partial.
That which is exhaustible and that which is to be abandoned by the noble ones is termed "limited."
If there are sentient beings who are to be tamed by the Tathāgata,
he explains it clearly for the sake of those of the two vehicles;
this was when the Tathāgata first manifested his transformation at the time of the ancient Three Refuges.
It causes deluded sentient beings to have faith in the Triple Gem.
Those who take refuge in the Tathāgata are those who [take refuge in] the Buddha of sixteen cubits.
Those who obtain the moistening grace of the Dharma...
This refers to practicing the Buddha's teachings.
One who gives rise to a mind of faith and joy believes in the existence of wholesome dharmas and noble beings.
One who takes refuge in the Saṃgha upholds two refuges:
the One Vehicle is the Dharma, and the noble ones of the Three Vehicles are the Saṃgha.
These three refuges are designated as the Dharma and the Saṃgha.
By citing these two refuges, the refuge in the Buddha is clarified.
As for the statement that "one who does not take these two as their refuge is not taking refuge in the Tathāgata," the phrase "this is not" mentioned above refers to this [latter case].
To clarify that those who formerly took refuge in the Dharma and the Saṃgha did not realize they were taking refuge in the Dharma-body Tathāgata— rather than merely the six-foot [physical form]—
it is said that taking refuge in the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is to take refuge in the Tathāgata.
The eternally abiding Dharma-body is called the Ultimate Heaven (Paramārtha-deva).
If one knows that returning to this is the true refuge in the Buddha,
these two refuges are the ultimate refuge in the Tathāgata as the Ultimate Truth.
Regarding those who take refuge in this Dharma and Sangha:
they know that taking refuge in the Dharma-body is itself taking refuge in the single essence of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Why is this so?
By taking refuge in the Buddha, one simultaneously attains the Dharma and the Sangha.
There is no distinction between these two refuges;
since their essence is not separate, by taking refuge in one, one obtains both.
The Tathāgata is the very embodiment of the three refuges:
the Greatly Awakened One is called the Buddha;
that which is to be followed as a model is called the Dharma.
Because its essence is eternally harmonious and compliant, it is called the Saṃgha.
Since the stage of Buddhahood is already perfected,
one does not receive a distinct name based on the individual substance of these three stages of training while they are still incomplete.

For those of the Two Vehicles whose knowledge is dull, the coarse and manifest distinction between the three refuges is taught; for Bodhisattvas whose knowledge is clear, the single essence of the Three Jewels as the Dharma-body is taught. Why is this so?
Why is it that there is one essence yet three names?

Those who explain the Dharma of the One Vehicle Path state that while the essence of the vehicle is one, the reason for the three is explained according to the capacities of sentient beings; thus, although the substance of the vehicle is one, it is spoken of as three to accommodate different people.
There are two reasons for citing this:
first, to substantiate the meaning;
second, to return to the fundamental source.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s four fearlessnesses:
this clarifies that because the Tathāgata possesses unimpeded realization and understanding,
he is able to teach the three [vehicles] according to the needs of individuals based on a single teaching.
If the Tathāgata teaches through skillful means according to their inclinations, this clarifies that the Tathāgata does not speak falsely;
it shows that the Teacher of Non-falsity and the Teacher of Skillful Means differ in their excellence, as they teach the three [vehicles] through different skillful means.
This is precisely what is called the Mahāyāna.
Although there are three names for the vehicles, their substance is in fact one and the same.
There are no two vehicles, nor are there any teachings of two vehicles.
As for those who enter the One Vehicle,
since there is no separate dharma,
how could they not be included under the designation of this chapter?
This "refugeless" refers to the One Vehicle;
it is the vehicle of the ultimate truth (paramārtha),
which is solely the Dharmakāya and has no other destination.
"The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas first contemplate the Noble Truths" is the title of the sixth sutra;
it marks the beginning of the Noble Truths.
To clarify that the truths have degrees of subtlety and coarseness,
one first distinguishes that wisdom has degrees of clarity and dullness;
since the truths are both subtle and coarse, [wisdom accordingly varies].
Learning also has its gradual stages;
first contemplating the coarse truths is designated as the beginning.
To sever all the dwelling-grounds (bhūmi) by means of a single wisdom—this is what is meant.
Because the wisdom that severs all fetters is identical and unimpeded, it is called "one wisdom.
Furthermore, another interpretation is that it is the wisdom that severs fetters by contemplating the single Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
To realize the merit of the four knowledges of abandonment through this one wisdom is [the meaning].
The knowledge of the destruction of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana-kṣayajñāna*) and the single liberation (*ekavimukti*) are one and the same name.
Furthermore, this single liberation is the knowledge that realizes the single truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*),
and it is also the thorough knowledge [of that].
The meaning of these four dharmas is that one clearly and distinctly perceives the Four Noble Truths. Furthermore,
according to another interpretation, if one wishes to contemplate the Truth of Cessation, one must first contemplate these four.
There is no such thing as the gradual attainment of the four supramundane, most excellent wisdoms, nor the gradual attainment of the four conditions;
this clarifies that the Buddha’s wisdom is complete and possesses no gradual progression.
There are two types of mundane [wisdom].
First, the fragmented body;
second, the dharma of transformation.
Because the Tathāgata has already transcended these, he is called the Great Being who has emerged.
The Two Vehicles are superior to ordinary beings, and the Tathāgata is further superior to them; therefore, he is called "the most supreme.

Because the objects and wisdoms—from the relinquishing of suffering and contemplating the origin, up to the relinquishing of cessation and contemplating the path—occur at different times, it is called "gradual."
The Tathāgata’s single wisdom perfectly illuminates all phenomena; it is not called a dharma that arrives gradually.
This is the supreme, unsurpassed wisdom of the supramundane.
The preceding section clarified that it is not gradual.
This clarifies perfect illumination.
The "diamond-like" refers to the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*).
This clarifies that the severance of fetters is not uniform.
The great wisdom of the two vehicles extinguishes all [afflictions], or rather,
it is the ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*) of those who have not yet reached the stage of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
This clarifies that the two vehicles do not sever the afflictions of the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*).
Initially, when one contemplates the coarse Four Noble Truths within the triple world, one does not yet attain the name of the first kind of wisdom.
It is by means of the non-dual wisdom of the Noble Truths that one cuts off all the stages of abiding.
This clarifies the Buddha’s wisdom.
Because he contemplates only non-action and no longer deliberates upon action, it is called "non-dual.
That all four stages of dwelling and ignorance are completely exhausted is termed the "various stages of dwelling" (*bhūmi*).
"Beyond the realm of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas" means that the profound and subtle stage of Buddhahood is not within the reach of those of the two vehicles.
"Inconceivable wisdom of emptiness" refers to this.
The Dharma-body is unfathomable and inconceivable.
That all afflictions are entirely eliminated constitutes the wisdom of emptiness.
This is ultimate wisdom.
The two meanings—the exhaustion of all burdens and the pervasive wisdom of tranquil non-action—are hereby concluded.
Thus, it is summarized:
first, the knowledge of the Noble Truths.
Those of the Two Vehicles have not fully perceived the principle and have not yet exhausted their afflictions;
they must now proceed toward the unsurpassed path to complete the wisdom of the Two Vehicles.
As for the meaning of "sage" (*ārya*), it is named "sage" because [their realization] is ultimate.
This clarifies that the names of the noble ones among the two vehicles are not yet true;
because their merits are meager and few, it is said that they possess only a small portion.
"Noble Truths" (āryasatya) refers to truths that are not those of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Having already clarified that the name "sage" is not yet ultimate,
we now clarify that the knowledge of the truths is not yet exhaustive.
The two vehicles do not yet understand non-action and the boundless.
That which is not the merit of a śrāvaka is the path of exhaustion;
it is wholesome and capable of producing the wholesome.
This refers to the initial awakening and realization.
It is only when one first attains Buddhahood that one fully realizes this exhaustion [of all phenomena].
To "reveal, show, and expound" means to speak for the sake of those who do not yet know, so as to bring them understanding.
This refers to explaining the profound meaning that is subtle and difficult to comprehend.
The phenomena of conditioned dharmas are manifold in their characteristics;
according to their types, they may be categorized as coarse or subtle, thus forming two classes.
The first is the coarse and manifest.
The second is subtlety.
The fetters and bonds of the three realms are called coarse;
this dharma of sensation is called coarse because it is so pervasive.
That suffering can arise is called "origination" (samudaya).
The point of its cessation is called "extinction" (nirodha).
To observe and know it is called the "path" (mārga).
These four are taught for the sake of those of the Two Vehicles.

The dharmas observed from the eighth stage of the vehicle of the *dharmakāya* up to the *vajracitta* (diamond-mind), which are not bound to the three realms, are called "subtle. Because these dharmas are extremely profound, they are termed "subtle."
That which can produce suffering is called "origination" (samudaya);
the state of its cessation is called "extinction" (nirodha);
and the wisdom of contemplation is called the "path" (mārga).
The unconditioned state of Buddhahood also enters into the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Its principle is profound and its meaning far-reaching; it cannot be known except by a Great Being (*mahāsattva*), for it is not something subtle that can be grasped through mere emptiness.
"Not within the realm of discursive thought" means that it cannot be taken as an object by the conceivable wisdom of the two vehicles.
"That which is known by the wise" means that only through the wisdom that eliminates the four abiding fetters and through the light of penetrating insight can one understand it.
That which all the world cannot believe,
that which causes one to revolve through the six realms of existence,
and that which cannot be known as the truth of non-action— [these are the truths].
This so-called "profound treasury of the Tathāgata" is another name for Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Its essence is unchanging, and thus it is termed "nature."
It contains all virtues and serves as a treasury;
it is explained as such because it is subsumed within the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
"The Tathāgatagarbha is the realm of the Tathāgata" means:
This is the title of the seventh sutra.
Only the Buddha understands it clearly.
As for those with immeasurable afflictions:
The eighth sutra begins:
"The accumulation of all afflictions constitutes the storehouse (garbha).
That which is enveloped by these is the Tathāgatagarbha."
This is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings.
Regarding the fact that the Dharma-body is likewise free from doubt:

those who can believe in the Buddha-nature of the Tathāgata, or who possess the great luminous nature that enables them to overcome the afflictions of sentient beings, will certainly be able to believe and know it through an understanding free from doubt.
There is a great illumination.
Regarding those who have completed the exposition of the Tathāgatagarbha and its skillful means,
and who have no doubt concerning the two natures.
One will certainly be able to skillfully explain it for others.
This refers to the two noble ones: the one of faith and the one of understanding.
There are two natures of understanding.
One is able to understand two kinds of truths.
Knowing the truth of conditioned activity (*nirmāṇa-satya*) is called the Buddha-nature of sentient beings;
understanding the truth of the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra-satya*) is attaining the Buddha-nature of the Tathāgata.
Since one knows that there are two kinds of nature,
one will necessarily be able to know that there are two kinds of truths.
Such [truths] are difficult to know and difficult to understand.
The following explains the meaning of the two kinds of truths.
Regarding the meaning of the noble truth of conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta-āryasatya*) and the meaning of the noble truth of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-āryasatya*):
that which can be cultivated is termed "conditioned."
That which cannot be learned is called "non-action" (avijñapti);
it is a synonym for "instruction" (vijñapti).
This refers to those who proclaim the four noble truths as having limits.
The fact that the causes and effects within the three realms each have a fixed period is called "having measure.
It is not because one can know all suffering and expound all paths through another's power;
this first interpretation arises from knowing a small portion of the Four Truths within the three realms through each respective teaching.
It is not by the power of one's own liberated wisdom that one knows all the four truths of non-action;
there are those with conditioned birth-and-death and those with unconditioned birth-and-death.
Since the truths are thus, existence and the cycle of birth and death are likewise so.
The ordinary person who revolves in saṃsāra without having severed the afflictions is called "existence.
The two vehicles, having already severed the three realms and the four abodes of ignorance, are called "unconditioned."
Nirvana is also of two kinds: with remainder and without remainder.
The body born of分段生身 (*duḥkha-skandha*) is called "with remainder.

One who, by means of their own power, knows that all suffering has been exhausted and attains the path of the cessation of suffering, thereby obtaining the Dharma-body, [is said to have attained nirvana without remainder].
Wisdom becomes increasingly clear, the power of self-understanding grows while reliance on the teacher's interpretation diminishes;
one ultimately perceives clearly, exhausting the principles of the Four Noble Truths.
This is what the Tathāgata refers to when he speaks of the Four Noble Truths.
Because they share the same name and accord with principle,
and because one maintains the four [foundations] according to the coarseness or subtlety of the dharmas, there are eight.
As for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, whose task is consummated:
The principle of non-action can only be fully realized by a Buddha;
it is not something that the followers of the Two Vehicles are able to investigate to its ultimate conclusion.
Why is this so? Why do the two vehicles not attain ultimate realization?
It is because nirvana is not attained through inferior, middling, or superior dharmas.
This explains the reason.
If the two vehicles were to attain the ultimate nirvana of non-action, they should be identical to that of the Buddha;
it would be without remainder and without distinctions of inferior, middling, or superior.
If one considers the śrāvaka as inferior,
the pratyekabuddha as middling,
and the Buddha as superior;
Therefore, we know that the two vehicles cannot attain the same contemplation of the truth of non-action as the Buddha. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata speaks of the ultimate perfection of phenomena;
this clarifies the nature of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because they are able to reach the ultimate state of non-action; "all Tathāgatas" refers to all Buddhas.
To "know all future suffering" means to know all phenomena (*dharmas*).
The future is difficult to know,
whereas the two [other] time periods are easy to understand.
For this reason, one does not separately distinguish all that is comprised by the afflictions or all that constitutes the origin [of suffering].
The four abodes, the arising of [afflictions] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and ignorance constitute all things.
All these are the dharmas of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
They extinguish all mind-born bodies and the aggregates (*skandha*).
Regarding "the realization of the cessation of all suffering":
because the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) is exhausted and even the final portion of the fragmented existence (*prādeśika-bheda*) is eliminated,
this expression is established with reference to that subsequent cessation.
It is not called "co-extinguished" because it is a dharma that undergoes destruction;
rather, it is not subject to the impermanence of fragmentation, mind-born transformation, or change, nor does it perish moment by moment.
What is called the "extinction of suffering" is the extinction of eternal permanence.
"Beginningless" means it does not have a beginning of birth.
"Uncreated" means it is not something produced through volitional construction.
"Uncreated" means it is not something produced through volitional construction.
"Non-arising" means movement.
"Inexhaustibility" means the absence of final extinction.
"Transcending exhaustion" refers to the characteristic of inexhaustibility.
"Permanently abiding" means being serene and tranquil.
"Pure by nature" means being free from all evils.
"Detached from the storehouse of all afflictions" is a brief description of a single type of ailment.
"Transcending the sands of the Ganges yet not being separated from" clarifies the Buddha-nature;
"not yet having escaped birth and death" means one has not yet avoided them;
"not yet liberated" means one has not yet avoided afflictions.
"Not different" means that it has not yet transcended and become distinct from the world.
That which is the inconceivable Buddha-dharma is the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Having explained the Buddha-nature, he now speaks of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
When practice is perfected and evil is eliminated, the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) manifests for use;
this clarifies the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
"The Tathāgatagarbha is luminous and not separate from the storehouse of afflictions" means:
This clarifies the nature [of Buddhahood].
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is not yet something manifested through accumulated conditions;
therefore, it is spoken of as the Buddha-nature of sentient beings within the section on the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
To clarify that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings and the Buddha-nature of the Tathāgata are identical in essence and without difference:
because sentient beings possess the Tathāgata within themselves from the outset, they possess the seed.
The wisdom of the Tathāgatagarbha is the Buddha-nature of the Tathāgata.
This wisdom of the emptiness of the Tathāgata is free from the arising of afflictions and all burdens of phenomenal characteristics.
To clarify this meaning, the preceding phrase is cited directly.
Regarding the phrase "Tathāgatagarbha," this term is cited again because it is intended to clarify that practitioners of the three vehicles have neither seen nor attained it.
"The two kinds" refers to the title of the ninth sutra.
The *tathāgatagarbha*— the Buddha-nature within sentient beings—
is one such kind.
The wisdom of emptiness is the Buddha-nature of the Tathāgata;
these are the two kinds.
As for the "emptiness of the Tathāgatagarbha":
If one is free from all that is said to be the storehouse of afflictions,
this is the wisdom that understands emptiness;
it is not empty of the inconceivable Buddha-nature of the Tathāgata.
This clarifies the buddha-nature of sentient beings.

Regarding these two types, the great śrāvakas who possess the wisdom of the emptiness of the aforementioned two natures have the wisdom of emptiness regarding the four abidings and the segmented [birth-and-death].
Bodhisattvas possess the great mind that hears the One Vehicle.
Those who are able to believe in the Tathāgata are Great Beings with clear wisdom who can believe in the Buddha’s teaching on the two kinds of buddha-nature.
All Arhats who speak of the transformation of the sphere of experience for those of the Two Vehicles,
although they are free from the four abidings and the death-and-rebirth of the limited分段 (paricchinna) nature,
have not yet been able to clearly illuminate and realize the Four Unconditioned Truths (catur-asaṃskṛta-satya).
They have also not yet understood the two kinds of Buddha-nature.
That which was originally unseen [by them] is vastly different from that of the Two Vehicles.
One is able to understand the two kinds of Buddha-nature within the truth of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*).
That which was originally unattainable is the absence of non-action within the mind while acting.
The function of the Buddha-nature has already been attained.
As for the statement that "all suffering is extinguished and only the Buddha attains realization," it means that all sufferings have been entirely eliminated.
Only a Buddha can do so.
That which is serene and eternally present may be called the True Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Those who cultivate all paths of suffering [realize this].
This refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
To exhaustively sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), one must possess wisdom.
There is nothing that surpasses the stage of Buddhahood for the fulfillment of the Truth of the Path.
"Three are impermanent and one is permanent" is the title of the tenth sutra.
It is not the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
That which is eternally abiding is taken as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Because the other three truths are impermanent, they are said to be "not" [the ultimate].
As for the single Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (*duḥkha-nirodha-satya*), it is free from the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
This is the title of the eleventh sutra.
Regarding the phrase "transcending the objects of perception of the mind-consciousness of all sentient beings":
ordinary persons lack wisdom.
How can this be known?
Furthermore, it is not within the sphere of wisdom of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas;
the inferior wisdom of those of the Two Vehicles is unable to comprehend it.
For example, one who is blind from birth is used as an analogy for an ordinary person (pṛthagjana),
who has not yet attained the untainted (anāsrava) insight into the knowledge of cessation.
Not seeing various colors— blue, yellow, red, or white— is like the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
The "seven-day-old infant" refers exclusively to those of the Two Vehicles (*dvi-yāna*).
Attaining untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is like the opening of an infant’s eyes.
One who does not see the solar orb,
though they know conditioned cessation (*saṃskṛta-nirodha*), has not yet realized unconditioned cessation (*asaṃskṛta*).
Just as a blind person sees nothing, ignorance is undifferentiated; it is neither called "is" nor "different.
That ordinary beings' consciousness possesses these two views and is inverted clarifies that the intention regarding ordinary beings is like that of the blind.
First, calculating in terms of annihilation and permanence; second, there are two inversions.
These refer to those who are "pure," clarifying that the vision of cessation by the Two Vehicles is not perfect.
"Extreme views" (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) explains the two types of views;
they consist of reckoning [existence] as either annihilation or permanence, and do not lack the middle way.
"Regarding the five aggregates of clinging" (pañcopādānaskandha): [text continues].
This enumerates the bases for views.
Regarding the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), one takes the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) to be the self;
through false conceptualization and attachment, that which is not the true self is falsely reckoned as real.
Regarding those who give rise to two views:
when one gives rise to a mind of two views concerning this self,
this is called "extreme view" (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).
These two views are called the "extreme views" (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
What are referred to as the "view of eternalism" and the "view of annihilationism" are the enumeration of these two views.
"Seeing that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" explains the severing of the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). This refers to those who,
seeing the five aggregates perish momentarily, claim they are extinguished forever.
Those who do not possess right view truly do not attain quiescence; therefore, it is said that they do not.
As for those who perceive nirvana as permanent, they consider the five aggregates—which exist only temporarily—to be eternally enduring.
They take this to be nirvana.
Those who do not possess right view claim that what is impermanent is permanent.
Therefore, it is said that they are erroneous.
As for the phrase "because of seeing through deluded appearances," these are all false and illusory, not true vision.
Regarding "the various faculties of the body," these refer to the five aggregates and the six sense organs.
Regarding "discriminative reflection," it refers to...
This refers to knowing the five aggregates and the six sense faculties.
It means seeing their destruction in the present;
that is, seeing the death and disintegration of the present five aggregates.
Regarding those who possess a continuity [of existence],
there is death here and birth there.
As for those who do not see [the path], they are either reborn in another region or attain the noble path.
Because this is not seen, one speaks of its eternal cessation.
The cause for the arising of abandonment depends upon this.
Regarding the continuity of the mind:
To clarify the view of permanence, one must first clarify the nature of the mind,
which is impermanent. Throughout the six realms of existence, from humans and devas, the moments of mind continue in uninterrupted succession.
This ceases and that arises, not abiding for even a single moment.
Those who are ignorant and darkened in understanding—
unenlightened ordinary beings— do not know this continuity.
Those who do not understand the realm of consciousness within a single kṣaṇa do not know that the mind arises and perishes from moment to moment;
they give rise to the view of eternalism.
They do not realize that they conceive of every thought-moment as being permanent.
Whether they go too far or fall short,
their minds are in fact impermanent, yet they claim it is permanent.

Regarding those who overestimate the mind’s reality: when the mind ceases and arises again, they fail to perceive its continuity and thus claim that a single mind exists eternally without change; this is called falling short of the truth. Regarding those who underestimate the aggregates (*skandhas*):
although the aggregates have not yet been exhausted, they claim they have already been exhausted; this is called exceeding the reality of the aggregates.
To be reborn after having ceased yet not being able to perceive this is called "inadequacy" (*aprāpti*).
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that to conceive of the mind, which is impermanent, as being permanent is called a "transgression.
To be unaware that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) continue in succession and are reborn is called "inadequacy."
Furthermore, there is another interpretation: one who observes the continuity of the five aggregates may claim that they are eternally extinguished, thereby contradicting the principle of continuity.
Such a person does not realize that while the substance of the mind perishes in each moment, it arises anew in the next, and thus remains unaware of the subsequent thought-moment.
Thus, they claim that [the view of] permanence is called "inferior" (*anupapatti*).
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that those who calculate [reality] as either eternalism or nihilism are all guilty of errors and inferior matters.
Those who are inverted are called "those who desire to explain.

Briefly stated, sentient beings perceive the five aggregates of clinging as having the mark of permanence where there is no permanence, and so forth, up to the mark of purity where there is impurity; these are the four inversions.
"All Arhats" refers to those of the Two Vehicles who have not yet fully realized the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Regarding all objective realms, they lack the Truth of Unconditioned Cessation (*anabhisaṃskāra-nirodha-satya*), which takes the Wisdom of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) as its object.
As for the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body,
the Dharma-body is the unconditioned entry into the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).
That which was originally not seen—

The followers of the Two Vehicles have only recently begun to practice the contemplation of conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta-karman*), yet they are not yet able to contemplate unconditioned cessation (*asaṃskṛta-nirodha*).
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, out of faith in the Buddha’s words, speak of the perfection of purity (*śubha-pāramitā*).
This clarifies that the Bodhisattva is able to believe, understand, and know cessation without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra-nirodha*).
This is called "right view.
The essence of the Dharma-body is eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
To form such an understanding may be considered truly authentic.
A "true son" is one who perceives the correct principle and thus becomes a true disciple among the noble ones.
One who has obtained the remaining wealth of the Dharma.
Within the teachings of the Three Vehicles concerning impermanence,
one is finally able to hear of the eternally abiding Mahāyāna; thus,
it should be known that this sutra must precede the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* sūtras.
Regarding the phrase "the World-Honored One of Pure Wisdom":
this clarifies that those of the Two Vehicles are necessarily able to understand and know the unconditioned (anabhisamskāra) Truth of Cessation;
they attain purity by being free from the afflictions of the four abodes (catvāra āśrayāḥ).
Regarding the phrase "it is still not within their realm":
for those of the Two Vehicles, although they have begun to sever the four abodes of the three realms, they still possess residual karma and afflictions, and the final body remains.
At that time, they are as yet unable to contemplate the truth of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-satya*).
How much more so for the wisdom of the four reliances!
The contemplation of the four as truths is the wisdom regarding birth and death;
this is merely using the superior to illustrate the inferior.
Why is this? Why is it that one practices the wisdom of the truths rather than the wisdom of non-action regarding the truths?
Those who engage in the initial practice of the Three Vehicles should not be deluded regarding that meaning; they should awaken to it and attain it.
This explains why [the Buddha] did not know:
having cast off the final body and attained the transformative Dharma-body,
he would then have known that birth and death were not yet exhausted and his contemplation of the Truths was not yet complete.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the truths and cultivate all wholesome practices directed toward the nirvāṇa of the Buddha.
